event.active_generic_land_01_social_borr: You nod. Their lie immediately becomes a local story.
Confirm it for now
They turn your correction into further proof of your supposed closeness.
The crowd understands the lie without you needing to crush them.
Your correction sounds like a public humiliation; the crowd leans in.
You draw the line without ridiculing them before their neighbors.
Correct them gently
You let them talk until they shrink their own story by half.
You wait; they contradict themselves in front of their neighbors.
They embellish long enough that some people start believing them.
You snap at the worst moment, turning the scene into a public reckoning.
Let them overplay it
You simply say no. The silence forces the braggart to speak again.
Say no plainly
A neighborhood braggart tells a small crowd that they are your close companion. When they see you arrive, they call you by name and ask you to confirm the story.
The Friend You Don’t Know
You ask them to finish the adventure without helping. The crowd waits for details.
Make them tell the ending
You add absurd details yourself; the braggart finally realizes you are mocking them.
Bluff along
You correct the facts one by one until almost none of their story remains.
Correct the adventure
To save face, the braggart now describes an entire adventure you supposedly shared. The crowd laughs, cheers, and demands the ending.
The Invented Adventure
You make them publicly admit they used your name to impress the neighbors.
Demand an admission
You frame the story as a joke that grew too large and give them a way out.
Give them a way out
You declare the story false but good enough to be told as a tale.
Turn it into a tale
A member of their family appears on a balcony, visibly mortified, and confirms they have never met you. The braggart finally lowers their eyes before the whole neighborhood.
Family on the Balcony
event.active_generic_land_01_social_call: You refuse the solo but keep the circle going until the next verse.
Your rhyme lands flat; the silence lasts just long enough to hurt.
Your verse becomes the one everyone wants to repeat.
The crowd repeats your bad rhyme with far too much enthusiasm.
Your verse fits the refrain and the circle starts again.
You understand the song’s pattern and answer cleanly.
You answer at the wrong moment and cut the singer off mid-line.
You follow the structure, but it sounds like a lesson.
You follow the rule while surprising the singers.
You turn your turn into a group response; nobody stays a spectator.
On a public square, singers make every newcomer answer their refrain. When your turn comes, the music stops dead and the whole circle waits for your verse.
event.active_generic_land_01_social_cari: You calmly ask that your face not be used as a public signboard.
You turn the joke back on the artist with a few well-chosen words.
You strike the same pose as the drawing; the crowd laughs with you instead of at you.
You let silence do all the work. The laughter dies in waves.
A street artist unveils a giant caricature of you without warning. Passersby burst out laughing, then all turn toward you to see whether you will laugh too.
You hand the chalk back and refuse to co-sign the joke.
You add a caption aimed at yourself; the drawing becomes a shared joke.
You replace the mockery with your name without erasing the drawing.
The artist offers you a piece of chalk before everyone: if the drawing stays up, they say, you can at least choose the caption beneath it.
event.active_generic_land_01_social_cere: You keep the sash and step before the guests.
You refuse to be the only voice of the visitors and bring several people forward.
You place the sash on a resident who knows the ceremony better.
You return the sash to the elder before the custom binds you further.
At the entrance to a ceremony, an elder places an embroidered sash over your shoulders to applause. A neighbor whispers that here, wearing it means speaking for every guest.
You use the speech to return the honor to those hosting you.
You thank the community without turning courtesy into a commitment.
You promise only to return if your road allows it.
Once you are before everyone, the elder explains that every sash-bearer must end with a promise. The guests fall silent to hear yours.
event.active_generic_land_01_social_chil: You introduce yourself with the nickname. The children instantly win.
You clearly ask them to stop, without threatening anyone.
You offer an even more ridiculous nickname; the children abandon theirs for yours.
You join the chant until the adults start laughing too.
Neighborhood children follow you, chanting a mocking nickname loudly enough to draw people to their windows. Several adults watch without intervening, curious to see how you react.
You accept the group apology and send them off to play elsewhere.
You say the joke is settled and no punishment is needed.
You challenge them to turn the chant into a welcome for the next outsider.
An adult finally comes out and grabs the ringleader by the shoulder. They demand the children apologize to you and ask what punishment would be appropriate.
event.active_generic_land_01_social_danc: You bow to the circle and refuse to be its compulsory entertainment.
Bow out
You call the best local dancer into the center instead of letting them test you from the edge.
Call the champion
You catch a foot and fall hard in the center of the circle.
You miss the rhythm and bang yourself hard enough to feel it.
You keep the rhythm through the final clap.
You take the figure and finish it with your own move.
Match the steps
The circle immediately copies your move as if it had always been part of the dance.
The joke breaks the music without making anyone laugh.
The crowd laughs, mostly at you.
You turn the challenge into a group act.
Turn it comic
A circle of dancers suddenly opens a path for you to the center. The local champion keeps their arms folded while the crowd begins counting the beats aloud.
The Counting Circle
You yield the center and applaud the local display.
Give the champion center
You pull spectators into the circle until the duel disappears.
Make everyone dance
The champion takes the rhythm and leaves you chasing.
You collide, and the crowd lets out a huge shout.
You hold the same rhythm to the end.
You reverse the figure and make the champion follow you.
Take the duet
The champion finally steps into the circle and offers a hand. The crowd immediately changes rhythm: this is no longer an initiation, but a dance duel.
The Champion Steps In
You bow as the winner without asking for another round.
Take the cheers
You declare that the circle won, not either of you.
Call it even
You raise the local dancer’s arm; the crowd accepts the verdict proudly.
Name the champion
The music stops at once. Spectators shout different names and wait for one of you to accept, reject, or reshape the verdict.
The Circle’s Verdict
event.active_generic_land_01_social_divi: One detail in your speech reignites the quarrel.
You divide the credit precisely enough to stop the scorekeeping.
You remind them what both groups actually built together.
You credit a detail to the wrong neighborhood; protests erupt.
Name the shared work
You declare that the celebration does not need a social winner.
Reject the ranking
Your line sounds hollow; both sides boo it together.
You find a line both sides can applaud.
Each side hears your toast as support for the other.
Your toast becomes the refrain of the evening.
Toast everyone
You name the hosts. One side cheers; the other remembers your choice.
Choose the hosts
Midway through a neighborhood meal, the host hands you the cup and demands a public toast. Two rival groups each want to be named as the ones who made the celebration possible.
The Divisive Toast
You hand the cup back to the host and refuse to arbitrate their prestige.
Hand back the cup
You let the rivalry become a loud game instead of an insult.
Let the rivalry sing
You give both groups the same refrain; neither can claim it alone.
Make them answer together
As soon as your toast ends, both groups launch competing chants. The host looks at you as if the mood is now your responsibility.
Two Chants
event.active_generic_land_01_social_fals: You stumble; the crowd mainly remembers your name and the awkwardness.
You end the misunderstanding without humiliating the organizer.
The square quiets enough to hear your version.
Your words vanish under the applause. The misunderstanding grows.
Correct the crowd
You notice who in the crowd still bears signs of the rescue.
You immediately spot the person everyone overlooked.
You spot no one matching the story.
You point to the wrong person. Two strangers protest at once.
Find the real hero
You step down without playing the role forced on you.
Step off the stage
You bow as if it were all true. Your face becomes the story.
Take the applause

You have barely reached the square when a master of ceremonies introduces you as the hero of a rescue you never made. The crowd is already cheering, and nobody seems to be looking for the real rescuer.
Hero by Mistake
The comparison turns into an ego contest, and the crowd loves the scandal.
You make the story clear, and the crowd cheers the right person.
You put the facts back in order without stealing the floor.
The two stories blur together; nobody knows what to believe.
Compare the stories
You step aside for the real rescuer; the crowd immediately shifts its attention.
Give them the stage
You keep the stage just long enough to explain who actually acted.
Share the stage
A breathless craftsperson pushes through the crowd. Several witnesses suddenly recognize them as the real rescuer, and every eye turns back to you.
The Real Rescuer
You turn the confusion into an anecdote; the square laughs with both of you.
Laugh at the mix-up
You let the real hero finish without adding your name to the story.
Leave the last word
You end the ceremony by steering the applause back to the right person.
Toast the rescuer
Red-faced, the organizer still holds the speaking horn toward you. The real rescuer waits, and the crowd wants to know how this story ends.
The Last Word
event.active_generic_land_01_social_fest: You miss an obvious mistake; the crowd sees it before you.
Your verdict looks arbitrary and the murmurs rise.
You can cite concrete details to defend your score.
Even the losers admit you saw everything.
Judge the details
You hand the judgment to the crowd. The organizers lose control of the result.
Let the crowd decide
You simply name the best troupe and let the hurt feelings follow.
Pick the strongest
Both troupes accept the criteria before the verdict.
Each troupe interprets your rules in its favor.
You make the criteria simple enough for the crowd to judge with you.
Your criteria sound pompous; the crowd starts parodying them.
Set clear criteria

Two troupes have just finished performing when the organizers shove the score sheet into your hands. The performers are already accusing each other of favoritism, and the whole square is waiting for your verdict.
The Improvised Jury
You admit the score was not as clear as the crowd hoped.
Admit your doubt
You give both troupes one final minute under the same rules.
Offer a short tiebreaker
You repeat the result without reopening the contest.
Stand by the verdict
The losing troupe refuses to leave the stage. Its leader demands a second decision before the crowd, which is already jeering at every hesitation.
The Loser’s Appeal
event.active_generic_land_01_social_gest: You acknowledge the mistake without submitting to humiliation.
The elders find your apology too quick to be sincere.
Your apology is frank enough to relax even the onlookers.
You choose a word that sounds even more condescending in the local custom.
Give a clear apology
You repeat the salute precisely enough to make the elders laugh.
You correctly repeat the gesture just explained to you.
Your salute remains awkward; nobody knows whether you understood.
You repeat the wrong detail and the crowd groans as one.
Repeat the proper salute
You simply say you did not know the rule and have now learned it.
Own the outsider mistake
You refuse to turn a mistake into a spectacle of obedience.
Refuse the ritual
While greeting a resident, you unknowingly repeat a gesture reserved for insults. Three elders step in front of you and demand a public apology as the street slows down to watch.
The Wrong Salute
You refuse the wider debate and bring the scene back to your original mistake.
End it on your mistake
You acknowledge that their rule is still the rule of the street today.
Respect the elders
You say the custom can be respected without humiliating outsiders.
Side with the youth
A young resident cuts in: according to them, nobody their age enforces the rule so harshly anymore. The elders turn to you as if you must now judge their own custom.
A Disputed Custom
event.active_generic_land_01_social_hosp: You say aloud that hospitality is not a contract. The courtyard freezes.
Name the hidden price
You put down 500 Berrys for the meal and leave the courtyard without a social debt.
Pay your share and leave
Even the neighbors present admit you set the boundary cleanly.
You thank the host while clearly separating the meal from the feud.
Your refusal sounds contemptuous; the story spreads before you leave.
The host hears your refusal as an invitation to push harder.
Refuse without insulting
You publicly repeat their version of the old quarrel.
Take their side
The host dodges and immediately returns to asking for support.
Your question hits an old grievance everyone wanted to avoid.
The whole courtyard sees that the meal carried a social price.
You make them state in front of witnesses what they actually expect from you.
Turn the question back
After feeding you without asking for anything, a family seats you in its courtyard before the whole neighborhood. The host now asks you to publicly endorse their version of an old local quarrel.
Hospitality on Credit
You stay long enough to hear both sides without promising a verdict.
Hear both versions
You refuse the second trap like the first and leave the neighborhood.
Leave both houses
The courtyard turns into a shared meal before anyone can back out.
Both families speak at once and accuse you of setting everyone up.
No one wants to sit down first.
Both hosts agree to speak without using you as a witness.
Seat them together
Before the discussion ends, the family across the way arrives with a covered dish. They offer exactly the same hospitality and demand exactly the opposite testimony.
The House Across the Way
event.active_generic_land_01_social_last: You have a small bench moved over so nobody can read your seat as support.
You give the last seat to an elder and remain standing behind them.
You take the last seat and force both groups to share your space.
You keep your plate in hand and refuse to turn a chair into a declaration.
At a communal table, only one chair remains between two groups that have been arguing since the meal began. Each side gestures for you to sit on its side of the backrest.
You eat without responding to the appeals coming from both sides.
You point out that one chair has far too much power tonight.
You announce that each side gets one sentence before the other can answer.
As soon as you settle in, both groups start telling you why the other is unbearable. The whole meal slows down to hear whom you will answer.
event.active_generic_land_01_social_mour: You ask the lead bearer directly whether there is a respectful way across.
You cross before the rite ends. A few faces will remember it.
You change route without asking the procession to adapt to you.
You remain at the edge of the street until the last bell.
A funeral procession suddenly closes the street ahead of you. A bearer explains that, by local custom, outsiders must wait for the final bell before crossing.
event.active_generic_land_01_social_peti: They use your attention to perform for their supporters.
You give them the floor and trigger two speeches at once.
The crowd finally understands their disagreement is smaller than their banners.
You force each committee to summarize its request without slogans.
You return both pens and refuse to become their public endorsement.
You sign the first sheet offered. The other committee takes it as an answer.
Your wording replaces both petitions before you even sign.
You write a narrow enough statement for both groups to sign.
One ambiguous sentence offends both committees at once.
Each committee reads your text as a victory for the other.
Two neighborhood committees approach you at the same time before their supporters. Each offers a petition and insists that your signature will publicly show which side you are on.
event.active_generic_land_01_social_proc: The alternating procession becomes elegant enough to draw applause.
Nobody listens long enough to understand the rule; the shouting doubles.
Each group accepts alternating only if it goes first.
You get one step for each group, and the square starts moving.
Alternate their steps
You stand beside one banner. The other group immediately understands your choice.
Choose one procession
You refuse to let one group go first by status. Both leaders must answer publicly.
Reject precedence
You refuse to become living proof of a local priority.
Leave the square
You propose an order both leaders can defend to their groups.
The rule seems fair, but nobody agrees to yield first.
Your rule contains a loophole both leaders exploit immediately.
Your solution is so simple the crowd repeats it like a new custom.
Set a neutral rule
Two processions meet at the entrance to a square too narrow for their banners. Each leader claims custom gives them priority and asks you to visibly stand on their side.
Who Goes First?
You refuse the place of honor and leave them to apply their agreement themselves.
Decline to lead
You walk between both banners; the groups follow at the same pace.
Lead them both
You place both leaders side by side and make them carry the compromise.
Make the leaders walk together
Both leaders finally accept the same compromise: they will pass together if you lead as a neutral figure. The whole square waits for your choice.
The Neutral Guide
event.active_generic_land_01_social_queu: You refuse to move until the accusation is withdrawn in public.
Demand an apology
The accuser raises their voice and the whole line turns toward you.
Your explanation sounds like an excuse invented on the spot.
Even the accuser admits the misunderstanding was plausible.
You calmly explain why you thought you were in the right place.
Explain your place
You spot the small tokens that actually mark the order.
You realize there is a local rule, but not quickly enough to convince anyone.
You read the wrong signal and deepen the misunderstanding.
You spot the dropped token at your feet that proves where you were standing.
Read the queue custom
You step back one place and end the dispute.
Yield your place
At a public fountain, a resident suddenly accuses you of cutting the line. You thought you were following the local order, but a dozen people now wait to see who gives way.
Your Place in Line
You accept the mistake and the line resumes as if nothing happened.
Accept the apology
You only ask the accuser to withdraw the accusation before the same witnesses.
Ask for a correction
You turn the lost token into a ridiculous trophy and the line bursts out laughing.
Make a joke
A woman at the back of the line finally raises her hand: she saw your token fall. The accuser goes quiet, and everyone waits for your reaction.
The Token Witness
event.active_generic_land_01_social_rese: You publicly ask the elder whether the seat is truly meant for you.
You keep the seat under the assembly’s divided stares.
You leave the bench before anyone has to order you off.
You remain standing beside the bench until an elder decides.
At a neighborhood assembly, a young volunteer seats you on a bench reserved for elders. The younger crowd applauds the nerve; the elders immediately stop talking.
You return the floor to the elders and the meeting resumes its usual order.
You speak while making clear that the seat does not belong to you.
You joke about the price of the best bench; a few elders laugh despite themselves.
The eldest finally smiles and lets you keep the seat on one condition: since everyone has seen you, you will open the discussion before the assembly.
event.active_generic_land_01_social_roya: You ask that your reputation speak in place of a birth title.
You give only your name and refuse to invent a place in their order.
You refuse to be ranked before even entering. The guests immediately notice.
You take the lowest offered place and enter without debate.
At a royal reception, a steward blocks the entrance until every guest declares the rank they claim. The people behind you listen closely to your answer.
event.active_generic_land_01_social_rumo: Your correction becomes a new verse everyone repeats.
By defending yourself too loudly, you give the rumor a better story.
The crowd picks up your version and drops the old one.
You break the most insulting version without stopping the song entirely.
Correct the rumor
You add an even more impossible detail. The crowd prefers your version.
Embellish it yourself
You turn the mockery into a shared joke.
By laughing first, you take some of the sting out of the song.
You play along, but the nickname sticks immediately.
Your laugh sounds forced; the teasing becomes more personal.
Laugh with them
You do not answer. The song reaches two more streets before you leave.
Let it spread
A group of youths is singing a grotesque story about you in the street. With every verse, passersby add a detail, and your name becomes the refrain.
Rumor as a Refrain
You keep the least embarrassing version, and the crowd settles on it.
Choose the nickname
You accept the heroic version, even though almost none of it is true anymore.
Claim the legend
You start over from the beginning, this time leaving no room for a chorus.
Correct it again
An old resident interrupts the song with an even more flattering and even less accurate version. The crowd now has two legends to choose from.
The Best Wrong Version
event.active_generic_land_01_social_thre: You decline all three invitations with exactly the same words.
You spend 1,000 Berrys on equal gifts so you can decline without choosing a favorite.
You honor arrival order and accept the first invitation.
You promise a short visit to each house and turn the evening into a social circuit.
Three households send you invitations for the same evening at nearly the same time. Each messenger insists that refusing their table while accepting another would be taken as an insult.
